title: The King's Spirit Stirred
sum: In Cyrus's first year as king of Babylon, the LORD stirs the Persian king to keep the word given through Jeremiah. Cyrus sends out a decree, spoken and written: the God of the heavens has given him the kingdoms of the earth and charged him to build a house in Jerusalem, and any of God's people may go up to build it, helped by the gifts of their neighbors.

The heads of families of Judah and Benjamin, with priests and Levites, rise up, every one whose spirit God has stirred. Their neighbors load them with silver, gold and goods. Cyrus hands over the vessels Nebuchadnezzar had taken from the Temple, counted out by his treasurer to Sheshbazzar, the leader of Judah, who brings them up from Babylon to Jerusalem.
readings: Read as history

Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BC, and his Cylinder shows him returning deported peoples and their gods. A decree allowing the Jews to rebuild fits that policy, and the Aramaic memorandum of 6:3–5 gives a sober archive version of it. Historians debate how much of the Hebrew wording is Cyrus's and how large the first return really was.
Read as a new exodus

The chapter is told as a second exodus: God moves a foreign king, the people go up with silver and gold from their neighbors, and the holy vessels travel with them, as Isaiah had pictured (Isaiah 52:11–12). The same verb, 'roused,' is used for the king and for the people. Ezra opens not with heroes but with God stirring hearts.

views.H: God keeps his word through Jeremiah exactly on time and moves the most powerful man in the world to send his people home. The decree is a real Persian document, and the inventory comes from the treasury's records.
views.C: The decree is likely genuine in substance but phrased for a Jewish audience; the inventory, with its broken arithmetic, may come from a real list. The first return was probably modest, and the chapter compresses events to begin the book with a single great act of God.
views.A: The Cyrus Cylinder, Babylonian business tablets dated to 'Cyrus king of Babylon,' Persian titles like 'treasurer' (gizbar) and names like Mithredath show the Persian world behind the chapter. Royal permission and royal property (the vessels) mark the project as legal from the start.
views.J: Jewish tradition reads the chapter as the end of the seventy years and the beginning of the Second Temple era. The Talmud discusses how Belshazzar and Ahasuerus miscounted the seventy years (Bavli Megillah 11b–12a). Because Chronicles ends the Hebrew Bible with these words, 'let him go up' became a byword for returning to the land.
views.X: Christians read the decree as an example of God ruling history through kings who do not know him (Isaiah 45:4), and the return as part of the story leading to the second Temple where Jesus taught. Some Christian interpreters have seen Cyrus as a figure of Christ the liberator, since Isaiah calls him the LORD's anointed.

deep.b: Ezra gives Cyrus's decision twice. The Hebrew proclamation (1:2–4) speaks to the Jews, names the LORD, and invites them to go up and build with their neighbors' help. The Aramaic memorandum (6:3–5), found years later in the archive at Ecbatana, says nothing about a return. It sets the size of the house, orders the costs paid by the crown, and returns the vessels. Elias Bickerman argued that this is just what we should expect: a herald's announcement for the people and a dry record for the treasury. Others think the Hebrew text has been written up by a Jewish author from the official record. Either way, the book's argument rests on Persian law as well as on prophecy.

deep.title: Claude's theory: three rousings
deep.b: My own reading: the book of Ezra is built on three 'rousings' of the spirit. God rouses Cyrus to send the people (1:1), rouses the people to go (1:5), and, as Haggai tells it, rouses Zerubbabel, Joshua and the people again when the work has stalled (Haggai 1:14). Ezra 5:1–2 is the narrative version of that third rousing. Read this way, the stoppage of 4:24 is not a failure of the king's decree but a time when God's people needed stirring again, and the book's turning points are always moves of God's Spirit before they are moves of men. Commentators such as Williamson and Kidner note the verb's repetition in 1:1 and 1:5, and Haggai's use of it is well known; linking the three as the book's structure is my own suggestion.

echoes: 2 Chronicles 36:22–23; Jeremiah 25:11–12; Jeremiah 29:10; Jeremiah 27:22; Isaiah 44:28; Isaiah 45:1–13; Isaiah 52:11–12; Exodus 12:35–36; Daniel 5:2–4; 1 Esdras 2:1–15

settings.to: The Jews scattered through his kingdom, and their neighbors in every place
settings.when: His first year as king of Babylon, 538 BC, announced by heralds and in writing
settings.why: To give legal permission and an invitation: any of the LORD's people may go up and build his house, and the people around them are to help. For Ezra's readers it was the charter of their community, proof that they lived and worshiped in Jerusalem by royal right as well as by God's promise.
views: Genuine in substance
Bickerman, Williamson and many historians: a Hebrew version of a real proclamation, drafted for Jews in their own religious terms, as Persian kings addressed other peoples in theirs.
Shaped by a Jewish writer
Other scholars: the text reflects later Jewish wording built on the Aramaic memorandum (6:3–5) and on Isaiah's prophecies.

settings.what: The inventory of the Temple vessels
settings.by: The Persian treasury, through Mithredath the treasurer
settings.to: Sheshbazzar, the leader of Judah, who signed for them; and later the community that kept the record
settings.when: At the handover in Babylon, 538 BC
settings.why: To record exactly what royal property was released and who was responsible for it. For Ezra's readers the list proved that the vessels in their Temple were the very ones taken from Solomon's house, so their worship continued the old.

title: Every Family Counted
sum: A long register names the people of the province who came back from Babylon: eleven leaders headed by Zerubbabel and Jeshua, then lay families by clan and by town, priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, temple servants and the descendants of Solomon's servants. Some families and priests cannot prove their descent; the priests among them are kept from eating the holy food until a priest can consult the Urim and Thummim.

The whole assembly numbers 42,360, with 7,337 slaves, singers, and herds of horses, mules, camels and donkeys. When they reach the ruined house of God, family heads give gold, silver and priests' robes for its rebuilding, and everyone settles in their towns. The same list appears again in Nehemiah 7, with many small differences.
readings: Read as a record

The list reads like an archive document, with family names, town names and round totals. Its towns fit the small Persian province, and its many priests and few Levites fit what we know of the period. The differences from Nehemiah 7 and the total that does not add up show a list copied by hand many times.
Read as a statement of identity

Placed here, the list says who belongs to the restored Israel: families with roots, towns with history, clergy with proven descent. It names ordinary people as the builders of the new community. Those without records are not thrown out but wait for God's decision. Tamara Eskenazi sees the list as a sign that Ezra–Nehemiah is the story of a whole people, not of great leaders.

views.H: A true register of the families who returned under Zerubbabel and Jeshua, preserved in Temple records. The differences from Nehemiah come from copying, and the large total includes people the family lines do not itemize.
views.C: Probably a composite list of several returns, or a census of Yehud in the late sixth or fifth century, placed here to represent the first return. Scholars debate whether Ezra took it from Nehemiah or the reverse.
views.A: Persian administrators counted subjects for taxes and labor. The list's town names and its Persian title for the governor (Tirshatha) fit that world, and Babylonian tablets from Al-Yahudu confirm Judean families living in Babylonian villages.
views.J: The genealogies mattered for marriage and for priesthood in Second Temple and rabbinic law. The Mishnah lists ten classes of descent who came up from Babylon, beginning with priests, Levites and Israelites (Mishnah Kiddushin 4:1). The lost Urim and Thummim (2:63) became one of the five things the Talmud says the second Temple lacked (Bavli Yoma 21b).
views.X: Christians have read the list as a sign that God knows his people by name (compare Revelation 21:27 and Luke 10:20). The genealogies of Jesus run through Zerubbabel (Matthew 1:12–13; Luke 3:27), and the care over records here helps explain why those lists mattered.

deep.b:

echoes: Nehemiah 7:6–73; 1 Esdras 5:7–46; 1 Chronicles 9:1–34; Nehemiah 11:3–36; Nehemiah 12:1–26; Exodus 28:30; Numbers 3:10; Jeremiah 32:6–15

settings.what: The register of the returned exiles
settings.by: Temple or provincial scribes; the writer of Ezra copied it here (it also appears in Nehemiah 7)
settings.to: The community of Yehud: its families, priests and Levites, and the officials who needed to know who belonged
settings.when: Compiled from one or more returns between 538 and about 520 BC, or later; placed here to stand for the first return
settings.why: To record who belonged to the restored community, by family, town and clergy, and so who could claim land, serve at the altar and marry within the community. Knowing this purpose explains why the list matters more than the story at this point, and why families without records are named apart (2:59–63).
views: One caravan
Traditional readers: the families who came with Zerubbabel and Jeshua.
A composite or a census
Many scholars: several returns gathered into one list, or a census of Yehud.

settings.what: The governor's ruling on the unproven priests
settings.by: The governor (Tirshatha), probably Sheshbazzar or Zerubbabel
settings.to: The priestly families of Hobaiah, Hakkoz and Barzillai, who had no family records
settings.when: Soon after a return, before the altar was rebuilt as Ezra tells it; the date depends on when the list itself was made (see 2:1–70)
settings.why: To protect the holiness of the priesthood without passing a final judgment: they could not eat the most holy food until God gave an answer by the Urim and Thummim. It shows a community trying to follow the law of Numbers 3:10 when records had been lost in exile.

title: Weeping and Shouting
sum: In the seventh month the people gather at Jerusalem as one. Jeshua the priest and Zerubbabel build the altar on its old base, though afraid of the peoples around them, and begin the morning and evening burnt offerings. They keep the Feast of Booths and every set feast, even before the Temple is founded. They hire stonecutters and woodworkers and buy cedar from Sidon and Tyre, shipped to Joppa, as Solomon once did.

In the second year, Zerubbabel and Jeshua start the work and set Levites over it. When the foundation is laid, priests blow trumpets and the sons of Asaph clash cymbals, singing the old refrain of God's loyal love. The people shout for joy, but the old men who remember Solomon's Temple weep aloud. The two sounds blend, and the noise carries far away.
readings: Read as history

Worship at the altar could begin at once, but building had to wait for money and materials. Ezra's date for the foundation, about 536 BC, sits uneasily with Haggai and Zechariah, who seem to place a founding in 520 BC. Either there were two stages, or the writer has drawn later events back into the first years.
Read as a new Solomon

The chapter retells Solomon's Temple story in miniature: the seventh month, the Feast of Booths, cedar from Lebanon by sea to Joppa, Levites and singers in David's order, and the refrain 'for he is good, for his loyal love is forever.' The new house is the old house restored. But the weeping elders know it is not the same.

views.H: The altar was set up in 538 or 537 BC and the foundation laid in 536 BC, then work stopped until 520 (4:24). Haggai's 'founding' in 520 is a second start on the same foundation.
views.C: The writer has blended two periods: the altar and the first efforts under Sheshbazzar, and the founding by Zerubbabel and Jeshua in 520 BC. Many think the chapter's pattern is modeled on Solomon's Temple account in Chronicles.
views.A: The cedar trade fits the Persian period: Sidon and Tyre controlled the coast, and the Sidonian king Eshmunazar boasted that the Persian king gave him Dor and Joppa. 'The permission of Cyrus' (3:7) assumes a royal grant on file.
views.J: The Talmud says three prophets came back with the exiles to testify to the altar's dimensions and place (Bavli Zevachim 62a). The scene of tears and shouting is often recalled in Jewish teaching on the mixed joy of restoration.
views.X: Christian preachers often read 3:12–13 as a picture of the church: real joy in what God has begun, mixed with grief for what is not yet. Haggai's promise that the latter house would be more glorious (Haggai 2:9) has been read as fulfilled when Jesus came to this Temple.

deep.h: Who laid the foundation, and when?
deep.b: Ezra 3 credits Zerubbabel and Jeshua in the second year after the return. Ezra 5:16 credits Sheshbazzar under Cyrus. Haggai 2:18 and Zechariah 4:9 date a founding by Zerubbabel to 520 BC. Readers have taken four main positions: (1) Sheshbazzar and Zerubbabel were one man, and the foundation was laid in 536 and resumed in 520; (2) Sheshbazzar began under Cyrus, Zerubbabel came later, and Ezra 3 has drawn his work back to the first years; (3) a ceremonial founding in 536 was followed by real building in 520; (4) yasad, 'found,' can mean 'restore' or 'repair,' so the texts describe one long project. See the topics on Sheshbazzar and Zerubbabel.

echoes: 1 Kings 5:6–11; 1 Kings 8:2; 2 Chronicles 2:16; 2 Chronicles 5:12–13; 1 Chronicles 16:34; Leviticus 23:33–43; Numbers 29:12–38; Haggai 2:3; Haggai 2:18; Zechariah 4:9–10; Jeremiah 33:11

settings.by: The priests and Levites, singing in turn
settings.to: The LORD, before all the people gathered at the foundation
settings.when: When the builders laid the foundation of the LORD's temple
settings.why: To praise God's goodness and his loyal love 'over Israel' with the words sung at Solomon's dedication (2 Chronicles 5:13), so that the new house is begun as the old one was finished. For readers it ties the small new community to David and Solomon and to Jeremiah's promise that such songs would be heard again (Jeremiah 33:11).

title: Letters Against Jerusalem
sum: The 'enemies of Judah and Benjamin,' descendants of people settled by the Assyrians, offer to help build, saying they worship the same God. Zerubbabel and Jeshua refuse: Cyrus gave the task to them alone. The people of the land then wear down the builders, frighten them and pay advisers to block them through the reign of Cyrus and on into Darius's.

The writer then jumps ahead to show how long the opposition lasted: an accusation under Ahasuerus (Xerxes), and letters under Artaxerxes. From 4:8 the book changes to Aramaic and quotes a letter from Rehum and Shimshai warning the king that Jerusalem, a rebel city, is rebuilding its walls. Artaxerxes searches the records, agrees, and orders the work stopped until he decides otherwise. The officials stop it by force. The last verse returns to the Temple, halted until Darius's second year.
readings: Read in time order

The chapter is not in time order. 4:1–5 belongs to the years of Cyrus and Cambyses; 4:6–23 to Xerxes (486–465) and Artaxerxes I (465–424), and concerns the walls of the city, not the Temple; 4:24 returns to 520 BC. Read this way, the letters help explain the broken walls Nehemiah heard about in 445 BC (Nehemiah 1:3).
Read by theme

The writer has gathered a century of opposition into one chapter: offers that would compromise, discouragement, bribery, accusations and royal orders. The result shows that every stage of rebuilding met resistance, and that the community's survival was never a matter of course.

views.H: Traditional commentators such as Kidner and Fensham take the chapter as a thematic summary of real events, with genuine letters drawn from Persian files. The refusal in 4:3 was faithfulness to God and to Cyrus's terms.
views.C: Critical scholars agree on the thematic arrangement. Many accept the Artaxerxes correspondence as substantially genuine, while some think its formulas show later editing. Several see in 4:1–5 the returnees' side of a long quarrel with the people of Samaria and with Judeans who had never left.
views.A: The letters follow Aramaic letter style: address, 'And now,' body, and a report through the chain of officials. The titles in 4:8–9 are Persian and Akkadian, and the fear of a walled city in the west fits the revolts of Egypt and of the satrap Megabyzus around 460–448 BC.
views.J: Josephus and later Jewish writers identify the adversaries with the Samaritans (Cuthaeans), and the chapter became part of the long story of Jewish-Samaritan division. Because Ahasuerus is the king of Esther, Jewish readers have long read the two books side by side.
views.X: Christian readers have drawn lessons on perseverance under opposition. The refusal of 4:3 has been read both as faithful separation (2 Corinthians 6:14–17) and as a contrast with the Samaritans welcomed in Luke 10:33 and John 4.

deep.h: The order of the Persian kings
deep.b: The kings in Ezra 4 are Cyrus (539–530 BC as king of Babylon), Darius I (522–486), Ahasuerus, that is Xerxes I (486–465), and Artaxerxes I (465–424). Cambyses (530–522) is not named. Since 4:6–23 deals with Xerxes and Artaxerxes and the city walls, and 4:24 goes back to Darius and the Temple, most readers conclude that the writer arranged the material by theme. An older harmonizing view identified Ahasuerus with Cambyses and Artaxerxes with the usurper Bardiya (Gaumata), so that the letters would fall before Darius; few hold it now, since the names do not match those kings. Josephus puts the letter under Cambyses (Antiquities 11.21–30), and 1 Esdras places it between Cyrus's decree and the story of Darius's three guards (1 Esdras 2:16–30, KJV numbering), giving a different order of events for the whole period.

The Aramaic letters keep the form of real correspondence, and the Plain keeps that form. A letter names the sender and the recipient ('To Artaxerxes the king, from your servants'), may add a greeting ('Peace'), and then moves to the business with 'And now' (4:10, 4:11, 4:17). The body often begins 'Let the king know' (4:12, 4:13; 5:8). Reports quote earlier exchanges (5:9–16) and end with a request for a decision (5:17). Royal answers end with orders and warnings (4:21–22; 6:11–12). The KJV's 'at such a time' for 'and now' hid this shape; modern translations show it.

echoes: 2 Kings 17:24–41; Nehemiah 1:3; Nehemiah 2:1–20; Nehemiah 4:1–23; Haggai 1:1–2; Esther 1:1; Daniel 6:8; Jeremiah 38:4; 1 Esdras 2:16–30; 1 Esdras 5:66–73

settings.by: The 'enemies of Judah and Benjamin,' settlers brought by Esarhaddon
settings.to: Zerubbabel and the heads of families
settings.when: When the foundation had been laid (3:10): under Cyrus as Ezra tells it; about 520 BC, under Darius, for scholars who date the founding then
settings.why: To join the Temple project as fellow worshipers of the same God. The narrator's label 'enemies' tells readers how to take it, but the speakers' own words claim kinship, which is why readers still debate the refusal.
views: A sincere offer
Some scholars: the speakers were genuine worshipers of the LORD, Israelites and settlers mixed, and the refusal created the split.
A political move
Others: sharing the building meant sharing control, and the offer was a bid for influence in Jerusalem.
Under Cyrus or under Darius?
Ezra's order puts the offer early, under Cyrus; scholars who date the founding with Zerubbabel and Jeshua to 520 BC put the offer then too.

settings.by: Zerubbabel, Jeshua and the heads of families
settings.why: To keep the project in the hands of the exiles named in Cyrus's decree and to protect its worship. For later readers it marked the boundary of the community, though 6:21 shows the boundary could be crossed.
views: Religious
The helpers' worship was mixed (2 Kings 17:33), and the exiles would not share the LORD's house with it.
Legal
Cyrus's decree named the exiles as the builders (1:3; 4:3), so letting others in risked the permit.
Critical
Many historians: a struggle between returning exiles and those who had stayed, over land and power, told from the exiles' side.

settings.by: The people of the land (4:4); no writers are named
settings.when: At the start of his reign, 486/485 BC
settings.why: To accuse the Jews of Judah and Jerusalem before a new king. Ezra gives neither its content nor its result; it stands in a list showing that opposition went on reign after reign.
views: A separate complaint
Most commentators: a lost accusation, mentioned only to show the pattern.
Linked to Egypt's revolt
Some historians: timed to the Egyptian revolt of 486 BC, when loyalty in the west was in question. This is a guess.

settings.what: The letter of Mithredath and Tabeel
settings.by: Mithredath, Tabeel and their colleagues, perhaps with a man named Bishlam (see the note on 4:7)
settings.why: Its content is not given. It was written in Aramaic, the empire's official language, and the book uses it to lead into the Aramaic letters that follow.
views: A separate letter, now lost
Many commentators: a different letter from Rehum's in 4:8–16.
The cover for 4:8–16
Others: the note that introduced the letter quoted next, sent under these men's names.

settings.what: The letter of Rehum and Shimshai
settings.by: Rehum the chief official, Shimshai the scribe and their colleagues in Samaria and Beyond the River
settings.when: During Artaxerxes' reign (465–424 BC), when the Jews were rebuilding Jerusalem's walls
settings.why: To get the work stopped by warning the king of revolt and lost taxes. It uses the language of loyalty ('we eat the palace's salt') and appeals to the archives. For Ezra's readers it shows how their neighbors used the imperial system against them.
views: Genuine
Meyer, Williamson, Fensham and most commentators: a real letter, perhaps abridged.
Later composition
Torrey, and with qualifications Grabbe and Schwiderski: shaped or composed later, as its formulas suggest.

settings.to: Rehum, Shimshai and their colleagues in Samaria and Beyond the River
settings.when: After a search of the royal records
settings.why: To order the building stopped until the king gives a new order. The door left open ('until I give the order') prepares for Nehemiah, whom the same king later sends to build (Nehemiah 2:1–8).

title: The Prophets Speak
sum: In Darius's second year the prophets Haggai and Zechariah speak to the Jews in the name of the God of Israel, and Zerubbabel and Jeshua start building again with the prophets beside them. Tattenai, the governor of Beyond the River, comes with his colleagues to ask who authorized the work and to take the builders' names. God's eye is on the elders, and the work goes on while a report goes to Darius.

The chapter quotes Tattenai's report. It describes the great stones and beams going into the walls, and it records the elders' answer: they serve the God of heaven and earth; a great king of Israel built this house; their ancestors' sin brought Nebuchadnezzar; and Cyrus ordered it rebuilt, giving the vessels to Sheshbazzar, who laid the foundations. Tattenai asks the king to search the archives in Babylon and send his decision.
readings: Read as administration

Tattenai behaves like a careful Persian official: he inspects, asks for authority, records names, allows the work to continue and refers the question upward. His report is fair to the Jews. Nothing in the chapter suggests hostility, only procedure, and a Babylonian tablet confirms that a Tattenai governed Beyond the River.
Read as providence

The narrator frames the report with two notes about God: the prophets' word moves the builders (5:1–2), and 'their God kept his eye on the elders' (5:5). The paperwork of empire becomes the means by which God secures his house.

views.H: Haggai and Zechariah stir the people in 520 BC, exactly as their books record, and Tattenai's inquiry is a real episode, preserved in a copy of his letter.
views.C: Many critical scholars also accept the letter as genuine in substance, noting its fair tone and Persian vocabulary. Some see Jewish editing in the elders' long theological answer. The first-person 'we said' in 5:4 hints at a source.
views.A: Tattenai is attested as governor of Beyond the River in a tablet of 502 BC. The report's structure (address, greeting, findings, quoted answer, request) matches Persian administrative letters, and archives were kept in royal treasuries.
views.J: The rabbis counted Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi as the last prophets; after them, they said, the holy spirit departed from Israel (Bavli Yoma 9b). The elders' answer models how Jews in the diaspora explained their faith to authorities.
views.X: Christian readers have seen in the elders' answer a model of witness before rulers, honest about sin and confident in God's promises (compare Acts 4:8–12; 1 Peter 3:15). Haggai and Zechariah's prophecies of a coming king and a glorious house are read as pointing to Christ.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the language of the record office
deep.b: My own suggestion: Ezra keeps telling the story in Aramaic between the documents (4:23–5:5; 6:13–18), so that the reader hears these chapters as if reading the empire's own file. The community appears as a case in Persia's records, with officials, inquiries and decrees. The switch back to Hebrew comes at 6:19, the Passover, when the community stops being a file in someone else's archive and acts as Israel at worship in its own language. Bill T. Arnold ("The Use of Aramaic in the Hebrew Bible," 1996) has argued that the language changes in Ezra and Daniel are deliberate and follow point of view: Aramaic for the empire's view of events, Hebrew for the community's own. On his reading the return to Hebrew at 6:19 already marks the community's own voice, so the idea is his; what I add is the emphasis on the Passover itself as the moment the file closes.

echoes: Haggai 1:1–15; Haggai 2:1–9; Zechariah 1:1; Zechariah 4:6–10; Zechariah 8:9; 1 Kings 6:1; 2 Chronicles 36:15–17; Deuteronomy 11:12; 1 Esdras 6:1–22

settings.what: The prophecies of Haggai and Zechariah
settings.by: Haggai and Zechariah son of Iddo
settings.to: The Jews in Judah and Jerusalem, with Zerubbabel and Jeshua
settings.when: Darius's second year, 520 BC, after years of stalled building
settings.why: To move a discouraged people to rebuild the house of God now, rather than wait for better times. Their own books (Haggai; Zechariah 1–8) give the words; Ezra shows the result.

settings.by: Tattenai, governor of Beyond the River, Shethar-bozenai and their colleagues
settings.to: The builders and the elders of the Jews (5:9)
settings.when: At the building site in Jerusalem, about 520 BC
settings.why: To find out who had authorized the work and who was responsible for it, as an official would before reporting to the king. The question sets up the whole inquiry of chapters 5–6.

settings.by: Tattenai, governor of Beyond the River, with Shethar-bozenai and colleagues
settings.when: About 520–519 BC, after inspecting the building in Jerusalem
settings.why: To report what he found, record the elders' claim that Cyrus had authorized the work, and ask the king to check the archives and decide. For Ezra's readers the letter, written by an outsider, is independent evidence of their right to build.
views: Genuine
Most commentators: a real report, with the elders' answer summarized in it.
Edited
Some scholars: the elders' speech (5:11–16) has been expanded by a Jewish editor.

settings.to: Tattenai and his colleagues, and through them the king
settings.why: To show that the building was not a new or rebellious project but the restoration of an ancient house, authorized by Cyrus. They admit their ancestors' guilt and leave Zerubbabel out of the story, perhaps to keep attention on Cyrus's official appointee.

title: The House Finished
sum: Darius orders a search, and in the fortress of Ecbatana a scroll is found: Cyrus's memorandum, ordering the house of God rebuilt, its size set, its costs paid by the crown and its vessels returned. Darius tells Tattenai to keep away, to pay the builders from the taxes of Beyond the River, and to supply animals, wheat, salt, wine and oil for sacrifices and prayers for the king. Anyone who changes the order will be impaled.

Tattenai obeys. Encouraged by Haggai and Zechariah, the elders finish the house on the third of Adar in Darius's sixth year, 515 BC. The people of the exile dedicate it with joy, offering twelve goats for the twelve tribes, and set the priests and Levites in their divisions. Back in Hebrew, the chapter ends with the Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread, kept by the exiles and by all who had separated themselves to seek the LORD.
readings: Read as history

The Temple was finished in 515 BC, about seventy years after its destruction. The archive search, the Ecbatana find and the royal funding fit Persian practice, though some doubt the crown paid as much as Darius's letter says. The memorandum's measurements are probably damaged.
Read as fulfillment

The chapter gathers the book's threads: the decree of Cyrus is vindicated, the opposition becomes support, the prophets' words come true, and the house is dedicated with sacrifices for all Israel. The ending at Passover makes the return a new exodus, completed with joy, because 'the LORD had made them glad.'

views.H: Cyrus's memorandum was really found at Ecbatana, and Darius's decree is genuine. The completion in 515 BC shows God keeping Jeremiah's seventy years and Zechariah's promise that Zerubbabel's hands would finish the house.
views.C: Most scholars accept the memorandum as authentic in substance. Darius's decree may have been expanded in its religious details, such as the 'soothing' sacrifices and the God who made his name live there. The mention of Artaxerxes (6:14) is the editor's summary.
views.A: The memorandum format, the summer capital at Ecbatana, royal funding of local cults (as with Udjahorresnet in Egypt), prayer for the king (as on the Cyrus Cylinder) and impalement as punishment all fit Persian practice. Elephantine's own temple memorandum is a close parallel.
views.J: The dedication (chanukkah) of this Second Temple, and its rededication in 164 BC, gave Judaism the feast of Hanukkah. The Passover of 6:19–22 is the model for the community's festival life, and the 'king of Assyria' whose heart God turned is read as a sign of God's rule over empires.
views.X: Christians see this Temple, later rebuilt by Herod, as the house Jesus called 'my Father's house' (John 2:16), where he taught and which he said would be destroyed (Mark 13:2). The Passover of the returned exiles anticipates the Passover at which Jesus died.

deep.h: Why does the Aramaic stop at 6:18?
deep.b: The Aramaic section ends with the priests and Levites in their divisions (6:18), and the Passover is told in Hebrew (6:19–22). Some scholars think the writer simply returned to Hebrew when his Aramaic source ended. Others think the change is deliberate: the Persian story of permissions and letters is finished, and Israel's own worship is told in Israel's own language. See the spec box on chapter 5.

echoes: 1 Kings 6:2; 1 Kings 8:63; Deuteronomy 12:11; Numbers 7:87; Exodus 12:1–20; Exodus 12:48; 2 Chronicles 30:1–27; 2 Chronicles 35:1–19; Haggai 2:18; Zechariah 1:12; Zechariah 4:9; Jeremiah 29:7; John 10:22

settings.to: The archive, and the officials who would carry out the order
settings.when: Cyrus's first year, 538 BC; found under Darius about 519 BC
settings.why: To record a royal decision: the Jerusalem house is to be rebuilt at royal cost, with set dimensions and the vessels restored. Its discovery settles Tattenai's question and turns the inquiry in the Jews' favor.
views: Genuine
Bickerman, de Vaux, Williamson and most historians: a real archive memorandum.
Doubtful
A minority: written later to support Jewish claims; the odd dimensions are cited both for and against.

settings.to: Tattenai, Shethar-bozenai and the officials of Beyond the River
settings.when: After the memorandum was found, about 519 BC
settings.why: To confirm Cyrus's order, forbid interference, pay the builders and the daily sacrifices from provincial taxes, and secure prayers for the king and his sons, with a curse on anyone who changes it. For Ezra's readers it showed that the empire itself guaranteed their Temple.
views: Genuine in substance
Most commentators, noting Persian funding of temples elsewhere.
Expanded
Some scholars: the religious language suggests Jewish drafting or later editing.
